extracted.intended_audience: EPA staff, state environmental agencies, regulated entities (power plants), and environmental / administrative lawyers and stakeholders participating in notice-and-comment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for identifying the "best system of emission reduction (BSER) adequately demonstrated" under Clean Air Act section 111, and for promulgating emission guidelines and reviewing state plans for existing sources (including required state data submissions and RULOF considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated (what counts as "adequately demonstrated")
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA may determine a system of emission reduction to be "adequately demonstrated" even if the system is not in widespread commercial use, so long as the system is not "purely theoretical or experimental" and can be reasonably projected to achieve the standard based on available data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may rely on extrapolation from pilot projects or individual commercial-scale sources; an adequately demonstrated standard "may reflect the EPA's reasonable projection of what that particular system may be expected to achieve going forward" (citing Ruckelshaus). The agency may compensate for a shortage of data through other qualitative methods, including reasonable extrapolation of a technology's performance in other industries, but may not base determinations on "mere speculation or conjecture." Legislative history anticipated the EPA's determination may be technology-forcing; nothing requires the technology be in widespread U.S. commercial use at promulgation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extrapolation and representative data
rubrics_metrics.description: To support an achievable standard, the EPA may extrapolate from available testing and must establish that the test data relied upon are representative of potential industry-wide performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have upheld standards based on systems that had not regularly achieved the standard in testing (e.g., Ruckelshaus). Where data are unavailable, EPA cannot rely on speculation, but may use reasonable extrapolation from performance in other industries or related source types (e.g., extrapolating SCR performance from utility boilers to industrial boilers in Lignite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance timeframe / lead time (achievability across the industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must demonstrate that the industry can deploy the identified system at scale within the compliance timeframe; reasonable lead time must be provided to design, acquire, install, test, and operate controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize needs for development of skilled labor, materials, and specialty parts. EPA has historically allowed phased compliance (e.g., stepped compliance approaches over 1–5 years), and existing regulatory performance-test timing (40 CFR 60.8: tests within 60–180 days after achieving maximum production rate or initial startup) evidences longstanding recognition of lead time needs. Examples: 2015 residential wood heaters, 2023 oil and gas NSPS (1-year lead times for certain equipment, 24 months for end of routine flaring requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of achieving the emission reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must take into account 'the cost of achieving [the emission] reduction' when determining the BSER, avoiding standards whose costs would be 'excessive' or 'unreasonable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has discretion in how it accounts for costs and in balancing costs with other BSER factors. The Agency frequently uses cost-effectiveness metrics ($ per ton removed) and, for the power sector, $/MWh metrics showing dollar increase in cost of electricity due to controls. Courts have upheld standards entailing significant costs where costs are viewed as normal business expenses (citing Essex Chemical, Portland Cement, Sierra Club v. Costle). EPA may look at multiple cost metrics and other cost evaluations to assess cost reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-air-quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must account for any non-air quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements in determining the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These may include disposal impacts of control byproducts, water requirements of control equipment, and effects on a source's own energy needs. Courts (Portland Cement Ass'n) have held EPA should consider counter-productive environmental effects (e.g., water harm) and energy impacts; the statute explicitly requires consideration of such impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration at sector, regional, or national scale (not just plant-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may consider factors on a national or regional level and over time—rather than only plant-specific conditions at the time of rulemaking—when determining the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: D.C. Circuit precedent (Sierra Club v. Costle) supports the use of a long-term lens that weighs future costs, environmental and energy effects of different technological systems. EPA may assess impacts on the electricity system's reliability regionally or nationally and reject controls that create reliability risks. The weight assigned to factors is within EPA's discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Best' requires balancing multiple concerns and agency discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'best' authorizes EPA to weigh competing interests (environmental benefits, energy needs, economic disruption) and to consider factors beyond those enumerated in section 111(a)(1) that further the statute's purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts recognize broad EPA discretion in balancing amount of emission reductions, cost of controls, non-air quality impacts, and energy requirements; EPA must engage in reasoned decisionmaking and may give different weights to factors in different rulemakings. Precedent warns against adopting technologies that may 'do even more damage to human health' than the emissions reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of emissions reductions (quantitative consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must consider the quantity of emissions at issue and the amount of emission reductions a candidate system would yield when determining the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plain language of 'system of emission reduction' and case law (Sierra Club v. Costle) support incorporating the amount of air pollution and achievable reductions as relevant factors in choosing the optimal standard for controlling emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of technological innovation and expanded use
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should consider technological innovation and the potential for expanded use or development of technology as factors in determining the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history and case law (Sierra Club v. Costle) indicate Congress intended section 111 to create incentives for new technology through development of adequately demonstrated systems, expanded use of best demonstrated technology, and emerging technology. Considering innovation is consistent with reading 'best' to include technological advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achievability of the degree of emission limitation (conditions and representativeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard of performance is 'achievable' if a technology can reasonably be projected to be available to an individual source at time of construction and capable of being met under most adverse conditions that can reasonably be expected to recur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show achievability EPA must: (1) identify variable conditions that might contribute to expected emissions, and (2) establish that test data relied on are representative of potential industry-wide performance given the range of variables. While courts established these standards in the new-source context (111(b)), comparable standards should generally apply under 111(d) for existing sources, subject to BSER differences (e.g., retrofit costs). Technology must be technically feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: State plan standards must reflect EPA's determined degree of emission limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's emission guidelines must reflect 'the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the [BSER]' (taking into account cost and non-air quality impacts), and states must establish standards of performance for designated facilities that reflect that degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may express the degree as a presumptive standard of performance in emission guidelines. While state standards generally must be no less stringent than EPA's degree, states retain RULOF discretion to apply less stringent standards in particular cases (see separate RULOF rubric). EPA's general implementing regulations set the framework for review and approval of state plans; EPA approves state plans found 'satisfactory' and may promulgate a Federal plan under 111(d)(2)(A) where states fail to submit satisfactory plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: State evaluation process and required source-specific data
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying EPA emission guidelines, states must evaluate each designated facility (source-by-source or group basis), assess applicability/technical feasibility of candidate technologies, and submit specified plant-level information to allow EPA to review whether the plan is satisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACE Rule required states to 'evaluat[e] each' candidate technology and include a summary evaluation of 'the . . . degree of emission limitation achievable through application of the technologies.' Required information about each power plant includes: annual generation; CO2 emissions; fuel use, fuel price, and carbon content; operation and maintenance costs; heat rates; electric generating capacity; timeline for implementation; and other information. States may conduct unit-specific evaluations of HRI potential and applicability, and may choose technology-specific heat-rate improvement values within (or even outside) EPA-identified ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: RULOF (remaining useful life and other facility-specific factors) — when states may apply less stringent standards
rubrics_metrics.description: States may apply a less stringent standard of performance or a longer compliance schedule to a particular facility based on remaining useful life and other factors, but must demonstrate facility-specific reasons making achieving EPA's degree of limitation unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To apply less stringent standards or longer schedules, the state must demonstrate for each facility (or class) that the facility cannot reasonably achieve the EPA-determined degree of emission limitation based on: unreasonable cost of control resulting from plant age, location, or basic process design; physical impossibility or technical infeasibility of installing necessary control equipment; or other circumstances specific to the facility. The state must show fundamental differences between facility-specific information and the information EPA considered such that achieving the EPA degree or schedule is unreasonable. EPA's November 2023 clarifications to its regulations govern states' consideration of RULOF.

rubrics_metrics.name: States may adopt more stringent standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 116, states retain authority to establish standards of performance that are more stringent than EPA's presumptive standards in emission guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States must include such more-stringent standards in their state plans and submit them to EPA for review under the Agency's implementing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that emission guidelines and rules identify the BSER and degree of emission limitation with adequate guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: An EPA rule must specifically identify the BSER and the 'degree of emission limitation achievable' (or provide sufficient guidance) so that states can develop approvable state plans; failure to do so is a basis for repeal or invalidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ACE Rule was found to have described only a broad range of values as the 'degree of emission limitation achievable' without providing adequate guidance for states; EPA concluded that failing to identify the BSER or a clear degree of limitation undermines state plan approvability and justified repeal. Rules should provide clear presumptive standards or sufficient methodology for states to determine standards of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of candidate technologies for meaningful emission reductions and adverse effects (e.g., rebound effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting a BSER, EPA should evaluate whether candidate technologies will produce meaningful net emission reductions and consider potential countervailing effects (such as a 'rebound effect' that could increase emissions for subsets of sources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACE Rule experience: HRI suite projected less-than-1% sector CO2 reduction and, for some states, a modeled increase in CO2 due to rebound effects. EPA relied on updated technical assessments (e.g., Sargent & Lundy 2023) showing less effectiveness than earlier reports and evidence that many sources already optimized HRI, limiting remaining opportunities. If candidate measures produce negligible or counterproductive outcomes, they may not be appropriate as the BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of changed factual developments (costs, availability, subsidies) in reassessing BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may reconsider earlier BSER conclusions in light of new factual developments—e.g., changes in industry, control costs, or federal subsidies—that make alternative controls more available or less costly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, EPA determined that developments since the ACE Rule (industry changes, reduced costs, new federal subsidies) made CCS and co-firing with natural gas more broadly available and less expensive, supporting reconsideration of BSER determinations. Rule validity can turn on current factual record and reasonable projections of availability and cost.
